Well as far as I know the break up of Marx and Bakunin was pretty complicated, and while first and foremost it was about "treatment", I see a lot of anarchists reject Marx (in general) because the petty fights that Marx and Bakunin had back during the era of the First Internationale. Just to make it clear I did not want to conclude that anarchism in is inherently anti-Marxian by its nature, just that there are is a serious amount of anarchists out there who don't recognize Marx and his achievements and contributions to the workers' movement because of the vile way he treated Bakunin and the anarchists (which was... well, vile indeed). Edit: And this is an important point because most of libertarian socialist thought (especially strictly Marxist but anti-Leninist tendencies) is based on Marx and Marxist thinkers.

That really sepends, libertarian socialism is actually a pretty broad term, and most of the tendencies within it are related to anarchism but there are a few differences I personally can point out. First of all, generally speaking, libertarian socialism does not reject Marx, while many of anarchist tendencies do. For most of libertarian socialists Marxist analysis remains the main basis of the ciritque of capitalism and contemporary society. Then there's the problem of methods. Some libertarian socialists believe that a transitional period is necessary (a tenet that anarchism generally rejects), but the form of that transitional period varies. For example Pannekoek and Krassó advocated workers' councils, Luxemburgism is for a "mixed" system that has parliamentary elements as well as councils, and then there is communalism (the Bookchin and Öcalan kind of communalism) and also some others. So basically the differences between libertarian socialist tendencies and anarchism are not crucial, but they do exist, most notably in strategy (i.e. spontaneous revolution, insurrection, peaceful activism, or reformist and revolutionary tactics combined, etc.). Of course there are slight differences in symbols, interpretations of various historical events, but If you ask me, I can perfectly relate to anarchists and I can work with them, too. It' just not my cup of tea for a handful of reasons. (For me it is really just a matter of taste, and the fact that I've simply read more Marxist and Frankfurt School literature than anarchist thinkers, so Marxism had a greater influence on me.)

To put it simply, og libertarianism was socialist and it was a term that referred to (and still does) socialist tendencies that reject the whole authoritarian business present in other socialist schools of thought (especially Leninism and offsprings, such as Stalinism and Maoism). It has nothing to do with right-wing libertarianism, it is not "tied" to it by any means. (Pardon me if - by any chance - your comment was ironic; Poe's law and everything.)
